summary: GRN 866 is a GRAS notice for a lipase enzyme preparation derived from Penicillium camemberti (GM self-cloned strain AE-LGS and non-GM strain AE-LG) submitted by Amano Enzyme, Inc. for use as a processing aid in dairy processing, fats and oil processing, and flavoring production. The notice relies substantially on GRN 68 (non-GM strain, narrower use) by incorporation under 21 C.F.R. § 170.215, with the pivotal 90-day rat toxicity study (Kondo et al., 1994) carried over from that prior notice. The notice provides a structured equivalence bridge between the GM and non-GM enzyme, three-lot specification data, a conservative dietary exposure estimate, and allergenicity and mycotoxin assessments. Key evidentiary concerns include: (1) the pivotal safety study (Kondo et al., 1994) was conducted on the non-GM test article (LGK) and its public/peer-reviewed availability is asserted but not fully documented in the notice itself; (2) the manufacturing process description is largely incorporated by reference to GRN 68 rather than reproduced; (3) the notice references flavoring production as a condition of use in the conclusion and exposure table but this use was not clearly enumerated in Part 1.4(a); and (4) CPA mycotoxin concern for P. camemberti strains is acknowledged but resolved by non-detection data. Overall, the notice is substantively organized and the bridge between strains is well-supported, but several documentation and incorporation traceability issues require attention.

findings.title: Manufacturing process incorporated by reference to GRN 68 without reproduction or adequate description of changes
findings.summary: The notice states that the manufacturing process 'was provided in GRN 68 and is incorporated herein' and describes only minor changes (reduced fermentation hours, lower harvest optical density, added coarse-filtering step, optimized microfiltration). The full process description is not reproduced in GRN 866. While 21 C.F.R. § 170.215 permits incorporation by reference, the notice does not identify which specific pages or sections of GRN 68 contain the process description beyond a parenthetical reference to 'Appendix I, located at page 13 of GRN 68.' The changes introduced for the GM strain (AE-LGS) and their potential impact on impurity profile or enzyme purity are not systematically evaluated in the notice body.
findings.recommendedAction: Reproduce or summarize the complete manufacturing process for both AE-LG and AE-LGS strains within GRN 866, explicitly identify all process changes relative to GRN 68, and evaluate whether those changes affect the impurity or safety profile of the enzyme preparation.

findings.title: Pivotal toxicity study used a less-purified non-GM test article (LGK); bridge to GM enzyme preparation (LGS) is partially but not fully established
findings.summary: The pivotal 90-day rat study used LGK, described as 'Lipase G Amano 50 (LGK) produced by the commercial process without the final purification and dilution steps.' The target material is Lipase GS Amano 250G from the GM strain AE-LGS. The notice provides SDS-PAGE, enzymatic activity, TOS content, and physicochemical comparisons between AE-LG and AE-LGS enzyme preparations, supporting protein identity. However, the test article (LGK) had an ash content of 22.2% versus 2.5% mean for non-GM commercial batches and 2.52% for the GM batch, indicating LGK was a cruder intermediate. The notice does not systematically address whether the higher ash and lower purity of LGK relative to the commercial GM preparation affects the toxicological read-across, nor does it address potential differences in non-lipase protein impurities between the GM and non-GM commercial preparations.
findings.recommendedAction: Provide a structured test-article bridge document comparing LGK (test article), Lipase G Amano 50 (non-GM commercial), and Lipase GS Amano 250G (GM commercial) across identity, composition, impurity profile, and processing stage. Explicitly address whether the higher impurity burden of LGK makes the NOAEL conservative or introduces uncertainty for the GM preparation.

findings.title: Flavoring production use included in conclusion and exposure table but not clearly defined in Part 1.4(a) conditions of use
findings.summary: Part 1.4(a) defines the intended uses as dairy processing and fats and oil processing. However, Part 3 (dietary exposure) includes a use level of 10 to 1,000 mg TOS/kg for 'flavor ingredient,' and the conclusion in Part 6.5 lists '(2) flavoring production (i.e., production of flavor ingredients for a wide variety of foods and drinks)' as a distinct intended use. This use is not described in Part 1.4(a) or the cover letter, creating an internal inconsistency regarding the scope of conditions of use covered by the notice.
findings.recommendedAction: Reconcile the conditions of use across all parts of the notice. If flavoring production is an intended use, add a complete description in Part 1.4(a) including substrate, use level, and food categories. If it is not intended to be covered, remove it from the exposure table and conclusion.

findings.title: Flavoring production use level included in exposure narrative but excluded from the conservative EDI calculation without adequate justification
findings.summary: The dietary exposure section states use levels of 10 to 1,000 mg TOS/kg for flavor ingredients but the EDI calculation uses only the dairy and fats/oil processing maximum (76 mg TOS/kg finished food). The notice does not calculate or bound the EDI contribution from flavoring production use, nor does it explain why flavor ingredients are excluded from the worst-case EDI. If flavor ingredients are used at up to 1,000 mg TOS/kg raw material and are incorporated into finished foods, the omission may understate the conservative EDI.
findings.recommendedAction: Either calculate the EDI contribution from flavoring production use and incorporate it into the overall EDI, or provide a documented rationale (e.g., negligible incorporation ratio, denaturation, or removal) for excluding it from the worst-case calculation.

findings.title: No published data on CPA production by P. camemberti U-150 (AE-LG); reliance on non-detection in finished enzyme preparation
findings.summary: The notice acknowledges that CPA is produced by multiple P. camemberti strains and that Ostry et al. (2018) called for further chronic toxicity and carcinogenicity studies. The notice states 'No published data were located regarding production of CPA by P. camemberti U-150' and relies on non-detection of CPA in finished enzyme batches (limit of detection 7.5 μg/kg by LC-MS/MS) to address the concern. While non-detection in the finished product is relevant, the absence of strain-specific CPA production data for U-150/AE-LG and AE-LGS means the safety argument rests entirely on end-product testing rather than a combination of strain characterization and product testing.
findings.recommendedAction: Provide or reference any available data on CPA production capacity of P. camemberti U-150 (AE-LG) and AE-LGS under fermentation conditions, or explicitly acknowledge the evidentiary limitation and explain why end-product non-detection at the stated LOD is sufficient given the processing conditions.

findings.title: Genetic modification characterization of AE-LGS relies on process description without independent molecular verification data in notice body
findings.summary: The notice describes the self-cloning process (protoplast transformation, non-homologous recombination of mdlA and pyrG genes) and states that AE-LGS does not contain DNA from a different species. However, the notice does not include molecular characterization data (e.g., Southern blot, whole-genome sequencing, or copy number analysis) confirming the number of insertion sites, absence of unintended insertions, or genomic stability of AE-LGS. The Pariza and Johnson decision tree analysis relies on the characterization being 'sufficiently well characterized' but does not cite specific molecular data supporting this conclusion.
findings.recommendedAction: Provide molecular characterization data for P. camemberti AE-LGS confirming the number and location of mdlA and pyrG insertions, absence of unintended genomic alterations, and strain stability across production generations, or cite published data supporting these conclusions.
evidence: Self-cloning process described (protoplast method, non-homologous recombination)
No molecular verification data (Southern blot, sequencing) cited in notice body

Using a pyrG-deficient strain derived from UV treatment of P. camemberti AE-LG as the host, transformation was conducted by the protoplast method to achieve the target transformant. The DNA fragments mdlA and pyrG were incorporated into the host genome through non-homologous recombination.

safetySignals.label: Cyclopiazonic acid (CPA) mycotoxin production by P. camemberti strains
safetySignals.summary: The notice acknowledges that multiple P. camemberti strains produce CPA, that CPA has moderate-to-high acute oral toxicity (LD50 rat oral 36 mg/kg), and that Ostry et al. (2018) called for further chronic toxicity and carcinogenicity studies. No published data exist on CPA production by the specific production strain U-150. CPA was not detected in finished enzyme batches at LOD of 7.5 μg/kg. The concern is addressed by end-product non-detection but not by strain-specific production data.
evidence: Le Bars (1979): 20 P. camemberti strains all produced CPA
Císarová et al. (2012): 12 of 14 P. camemberti strains produced CPA
Ostry et al. (2018): CPA is a potentially serious mycotoxin requiring further chronic/carcinogenicity studies
CPA not detected in AE-LGS enzyme at LOD 7.5 μg/kg (LC-MS/MS)
No published data on CPA production by P. camemberti U-150

safetySignals.label: Occupational allergenicity to P. camemberti reported in workers
safetySignals.summary: Two occupational allergenicity cases are identified: Marchisio et al. (1999) reported possible extrinsic allergic alveolitis by inhalation in a salami factory worker, and Merget et al. (2008) reported IgE-mediated asthma, rhinitis, and contact urticaria in a dry-sausage packer. The notice distinguishes these from dietary exposure to the purified enzyme preparation and concludes no dietary allergenicity concern. The distinction is scientifically supported by route of exposure, dose, and enzyme denaturation arguments.
evidence: Marchisio et al. (1999): possible extrinsic allergic alveolitis by P. camemberti inhalation
Merget et al. (2008): IgE-mediated asthma and rhinitis in dry-sausage packer
Notice distinguishes occupational inhalation from dietary exposure to purified denatured enzyme

citations.excerpt: Merget et al. (2008) reported the details of an employee who experienced progressive work-related asthma, rhinitis, and contact urticaria after contact with mold-cured dry sausages and had specific antiglobulin E antibodies to P. camemberti.
citations.section: Part 6.1 Safety of Penicillium camemberti production strains AE-LG and AE-LGS

citations.excerpt: The circumstances and route of exposure for the reported cases of allergic reactions in workers after repeated contact with high levels of P. camemberti used in finishing dried sausages do not raise safety concerns for dietary exposure to low levels of an extracellular lipase enzyme preparation derived P. camemberti and not containing the production organism.
citations.section: Part 6.1 Safety of Penicillium camemberti production strains AE-LG and AE-LGS

safetySignals.label: Pivotal test article (LGK) had substantially higher impurity burden than commercial GM preparation
safetySignals.summary: The pivotal 90-day rat study used LGK with 22.2% ash content, compared to 2.52% for the commercial GM batch (AE-LGS). The notice attributes the high ash to freeze-drying of the pre-precipitation liquid. The safety margin (399-fold) is large, but the impurity profile difference between LGK and the commercial GM preparation is not formally evaluated. This is a watch-level signal because the higher impurity burden of LGK could make the NOAEL conservative, but the direction and magnitude of the effect are not documented.
evidence: LGK ash 22.2% vs. 2.52% for GM commercial batch (Table 2)
LGK produced without final purification and dilution steps
399-fold safety margin between NOAEL and EDI
